title: You Hypocrite.
theme: The honesty to confront the hypocrisy within ourselves, the humility to help one another without condemnation, and the grace to turn back and walk with Christ again
opening: It is easy to say what we believe. Living it is where things get complicated.
prayer: Lord, show me where my life does not reflect what I say I believe. When I know better and do it anyway, do not let me hide from You or become comfortable with what separates me from You. Help me see the beam in my own eye and approach the struggles of others with the mercy I need myself. Give me the humility to admit when I am wrong, the courage to turn around, and a forgiving heart toward those trying to do the same. When I fail, let me remember that You have not walked away from me. Give me the grace to turn around and walk with You again. Amen.
body:
I remember hearing people talk about why they had left the Catholic Church, especially when I was younger. There were many reasons, but one that came up often was hypocrisy. It is an uncomfortable word, but let's call it what it is.
We profess one thing and sometimes live another. We speak about forgiveness and refuse to forgive. We talk about loving our neighbor and then tear someone apart. We say yes to God and then live as though we never said it. I understand why people struggle with that. I struggle with it too. But I cannot point toward someone else's hypocrisy without confronting my own. We all have wood in our eyes.
Today's Gospel seems to address this directly. A father asks two sons to work in his vineyard. One says no, changes his mind and goes. The other says yes but never goes. Neither son is perfect. The perfect response would have been yes, followed by action. But Jesus doesn't give us that son. He gives us two imperfect people, and the one who did the Father's will was the one who changed.
Sometimes we say yes and don't follow through. Sometimes we say no and later feel that uncomfortable stirring inside us: guilt, conscience, regret. Something tells us, I knew better. I knew this wasn't right. I did it anyway.
Catholicism has a reputation for guilt. Repent. Confess. You are a sinner. I understand how that can sound condemning, especially to someone who has already felt judged by the Church. But guilt does not have to say, “You are bad.” It can say, “Turn around.” The first son did.
Maybe hypocrisy isn't simply that we fail to live perfectly what we believe. We all fail. The danger is when we know something is wrong and keep doing it anyway. We justify it, hide it, or become so accustomed to it that eventually it stops bothering us. Our mouths say yes to God while our lives continue to say no.
But we don't have to hide that from God or from one another. I believe this, and I failed to live it. I judged. I was unkind. I was selfish. I knew better and did it anyway. And then I can turn around.
This is where the beam in my own eye matters. I cannot approach someone else's sin as though I stand above it. I have my own wood to remove. But recognizing that does not mean I stop caring when I see someone I love struggling with theirs. It should change how I approach them—not with condemnation or to expose them, but gently, because I know what it feels like to need the same mercy.
There should be room for that kind of honesty in the Church. A place where we can admit our sin without hiding for fear of judgment. Where someone can help us see what we cannot see ourselves. Where repentance does not mean humiliation, and forgiveness does not mean pretending nothing happened. Because what could be worse than failing and then walking away from the very place where we can be restored?
Maybe that is what I want someone who has walked away because of hypocrisy, guilt, judgment, or even their own sin to know. None of us is without the beam. None of us lives our yes perfectly. We are going to get it wrong. We will sometimes know better and do it anyway. But we don't have to hide from that truth, and we certainly don't have to hide from God because of it. We can see it, own it, ask forgiveness, help one another see, and turn around.
The first son had already said no, but his no was not the end of his story. He changed his mind. There is no hypocrisy in admitting we have failed. The hypocrisy is pretending we haven't.
God does not ask us to remain where we failed. He asks us to turn around and walk with Him again.
